title: 10 Investigating the effects of mixed condensed and hydrolyzable tannin extract inclusion rate on greenhouse gas production and diet digestibility using the in vitro gas production technique
content:
Abstract
There has been an observed increase in greenhouse gas emissions within the last century, and beef cattle production is a known contributor to this global issue. Several studies have evaluated the impact of condensed (CT) or hydrolyzable (HT) tannin extract (TE) supplementation for beef cattle on methane mitigation and metabolic functions, but fewer have evaluated the inclusion rate of a combination of tannin types. Thus, our objective was to investigate the effect of the inclusion rate of a mixed CT and HT extract (Silvafeed ByPro; SILVATEAM, San Michele Mondovi, Italy) on methane production and feed digestibility using the in vitro gas production (IVGP) technique. A completely randomized design was used to evaluate the inclusion of TE at 0.0, 0.3, 0.6, or 0.9% DM (TE0.0, TE0.3, TE0.6, or TE0.9) of a high-roughage total mixed ration across three 48 h incubations, with a total of seven replicates per treatment within each incubation. Fresh rumen inoculum from two ruminally cannulated donor steers consuming ad libitum bermudagrass hay was utilized for all incubations. Methane production was measured from all samples, while neutral detergent fiber digestibility (NDFD) was measured from four replicates of each supplemental treatment within each incubation. A random coefficients model was utilized for data analysis, with incubation as the random effect within the model. There was no effect of TE inclusion rate on total gas production or lag time before the initiation of gas production (P ≥ 0.11) for the exponential function, but the fractional rate of gas production of the exponential function was greater (P < 0.01) for TE0.0 than for TE0.6 and TE0.9. Based on the log 2-pool function, gas production of the nonfiber carbohydrate pool was lower (P = 0.03) for TE0.9 compared to TE0.0 and TE0.3. Inversely, TE0.9 had the greatest (P = 0.01) gas production of the fiber carbohydrate pool compared to all other treatments. Total methane production and methane produced per unit of fermentable organic matter were reduced (P ≤ 0.05) for TE0.3 compared to TE0.6. However, there was no effect of TE inclusion on NDFD (P = 0.21). Our results indicate that a combination of CT and HT extract included in the diet at 0.3% of DM may allow for reduced methane production without negatively impacting fiber digestibility. Ultimately, further research is warranted to determine the effects of the inclusion rate of this TE combination on in vivo methane production.
